sections.title: GitHub Enterprise Cloud/Server Compatibility Assumptions
sections.current_state: Rig Relay ships a GitHub provider integration module under rig_relay/integrations/github_provider/ that targets GitHub.com (cloud) via GitHub App authentication. The _capabilities.py module registers provider capabilities including repository scanning, code scanning alert ingestion, and PR mutation rehearsal. No explicit GHES (GitHub Enterprise Server) API version mapping or base-URL routing exists.
sections.gap_analysis: GHES compatibility is not a nice-to-have; it is a gated enterprise track. Rig Relay must support both GitHub Enterprise Cloud and Server with explicit configuration for api_base_url, hostname, API version/capability profile, proxy/custom CA settings, and installation scope. GHES instances use different API base URLs (https://<hostname>/api/v3) and may lag GitHub.com API versions by 6-18 months. The provider currently hardcodes api.github.com. No GHES version-detection handshake, no API-compatibility matrix, and no fallback to deprecated endpoints exist. Enterprise Server customers on air-gapped networks cannot use the provider at all.
sections.required_implementation: Add a GitHubConfiguration model with hostname, api_base_url, api_version fields. Implement a GHESVersionDetector that probes /meta or /rate_limit at connection time and maps the returned version string to a capability reduction profile. The capability manifest must declare per-endpoint minimum GHES version requirements. The LivePRMutationAdapter must degrade gracefully on GHES versions lacking checks API v2. The CodeScanningAlert ingestion must handle SARIF v1/v2/v3 differences across GHES releases.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprise RFPs will ask: 'Does the solution support GitHub Enterprise Server 3.9+? What is the minimum GHES version? Does it work in air-gapped environments? Does it respect our proxy configuration?' Expect SOC2 and FedRAMP questionnaires to require GHES support as a table-stakes item.

sections.title: Organization Install Flow
sections.current_state: The GitHub App registration path exists conceptually in _github_app_token_manager.py but an end-to-end org install flow (select org, request admin approval, verify installation, poll for completion) is not implemented. The OAuth consent flow in rig_relay/identity/ handles user-level tokens but not GitHub App org installation.
sections.gap_analysis: No org-selection UI. No installation callback webhook handler. No polling loop for pending installation authorization. No distinction between user-account and org-account installations. No handling of the 'request' action when the installing user is not an org admin. No installation token refresh lifecycle that respects the 1-hour expiry with automatic rotation.
sections.required_implementation: Build a GitHubOrgInstallWizard that: (1) redirects to GitHub App installation page with suggested target org, (2) registers an installation.created webhook handler, (3) polls /app/installations until the target org appears, (4) stores the installation_id in the github_installation Postgres table, (5) begins background ingestion for that org. Add a reinstallation flow for revoked/migrated installations. Surface installation status in the cockpit Provider Health widget.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How many clicks to onboard 200 repos? Can we use the GitHub App Manifest flow? Does the install require org-owner approval every time we add a repo?' Expect procurement to require a manifest-flow option and bulk-install capability.

sections.title: Repository Allowlist/Denylist
sections.current_state: No allowlist or denylist mechanism exists. If an installation spans 500 repos, all 500 will be ingested. The _capabilities.py and _operating_picture.py scan all visible repos without filtering.
sections.gap_analysis: Repository allowlist/denylist should be a P1/P2 enterprise gate, not optional polish. Without allowlist/denylist, Rig Relay would have visibility into repos that the enterprise has not authorized for tool access. Enterprise tenants typically want to exclude archived repos, forks, template repos, and repos matching naming patterns (e.g., *-legacy, spike-*, poc-*). Without allowlist/denylist, rate-limit budgets are wasted, DuckDB projections bloat, and security scanning surfaces explode. No per-tenant, per-org, or per-repo exclusion configuration exists.
sections.required_implementation: Add a RepositoryScopePolicy model with fields: include_patterns (glob list), exclude_patterns (glob list), include_archived (bool default false), include_forks (bool default false), include_templates (bool default false), min_stars (int), min_last_push_days (int). Store per installation. Install a filter in the provider packet ingestion pipeline that drops packets for excluded repos before schema validation. Surface denylist stats in the cockpit Repository Coverage widget. Add a repoadd/reporemove API to adjust scope post-install without reinstalling the GitHub App.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Can we scope to a subset of repos? Can we dynamically add/remove repos without reinstalling? Can we exclude repos by team or topic? Is the denylist auditable?' SOC2 auditors will expect evidence that excluded repos are never queried.

sections.title: Least-Privilege GitHub App Permission Profiles
sections.current_state: A single GitHub App configuration exists with a hardcoded permission set. The _capabilities.py and _github_app_token_manager.py do not dynamically compute required permissions from enabled features. No tiered permission profiles (read-only observer, read+checks, read+checks+PR mutation) are defined.
sections.gap_analysis: Per the capability manifest (etc/rig.ide.capability_manifest.v1.json), different features require different GitHub permissions. Read-only code scanning ingestion needs metadata:read, security_events:read, contents:read. PR mutation rehearsal needs pull_requests:write, checks:write. The current model is all-or-nothing, violating least-privilege. No permission-audit report exists. No mechanism to revoke elevated permissions when features are disabled.
sections.required_implementation: Define three GitHub App Permission Profiles: Observer (metadata:read, security_events:read, contents:read, issues:read, pull_requests:read), Reviewer (Observer + checks:read, actions:read, deployments:read), and Mutator (Reviewer + checks:write, pull_requests:write, contents:write, statuses:write). Each provider capability in the manifest must declare its required permission tier. When a tenant enables a feature that requires a higher tier, surface an upgrade prompt with a deep link to the GitHub App permission update page. Generate a Permission Profile Compliance Report that maps enabled features to required permissions and flags gaps.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Why does the app need contents:write? We won't approve write access. Can we install the observer tier only and still get value?' Security review boards will require a per-permission justification document. Expect procurement to demand the observer tier as the default with explicit opt-in for mutation.

sections.title: Admin Approval Flow
sections.current_state: No admin approval gating exists. The GitHub App installation is a one-time action with no subsequent approval checkpoints. The _governance.py mixin handles tool-level permission gating but not provider-level admin approval for org-wide actions like enabling PR mutation or expanding repo scope.
sections.gap_analysis: Admin approval flow should depend on signed, scope-bound approval receipts. Time-bound: approvals expire after configurable TTL. Scope-bound: approvals authorize specific operations, not blanket access. Enterprises require admin-approval gates for: enabling write-access features, adding repos to scope, changing permission profiles, enabling live PR mutation, and modifying branch protection reporting. Without these gates, a single operator could enable mutation across an entire org. No approval request/response flow, no audit trail of admin decisions, and no time-bound approval windows exist.
sections.required_implementation: Build an AdminApprovalGate with: (1) ApprovalRequest model (requester, feature, scope, justification, expiration_ttl), (2) ApprovalResponse model (approver, decision, conditions, signed attestation), (3) approval webhook that pings the cockpit Admin Approvals widget, (4) HMAC-SHA256 attestation signing using the existing attestation infrastructure from rig_relay/governance/, (5) a revocation path that rolls back features when approval is withdrawn. Store approval events in github_enterprise_audit_event with event_type='admin_approval.granted'/'admin_approval.revoked'/'admin_approval.expired'. Surface pending approvals as a red badge in the cockpit header.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Who can approve PR mutation? Can we require two approvers? Can we set approval windows (business hours only)? Does approval expire? Is the approval decision auditable?' SOC2 and ISO 27001 auditors will demand a change-management approval trail.

sections.title: Enterprise Audit-Log Ingestion
sections.current_state: No GitHub enterprise audit log ingestion exists. The _operating_picture.py and _provider_packet pipeline handle repository and security-event webhooks but do not ingest the GitHub Enterprise audit log API (GET /orgs/{org}/audit-log or GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/audit-log).
sections.gap_analysis: Enterprise audit-log ingestion must be content-light and tenant-scoped. Raw audit events must not leak into product telemetry. SHA256 hashing for all content-derived audit data. GitHub Enterprise Cloud audit logs provide a rich stream of org-level events: repo creation/deletion, permission changes, member additions/removals, OAuth app authorizations, SSH key additions, org setting changes. Without ingestion, Rig Relay has no visibility into org-level governance events that affect the security posture it reports on. Enterprise customers rely on audit logs for compliance evidence (SOC2, ISO 27001, FedRAMP). Missing this means Rig Relay's operating picture is repo-scoped only, missing the org/enterprise governance layer.
sections.required_implementation: Add an EnterpriseAuditLogIngestor that: (1) polls GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/audit-log or GET /orgs/{org}/audit-log with cursor-based pagination, (2) normalizes GitHub audit events into github_enterprise_audit_event rows (event_type, actor, action, repo, org, timestamp, raw_payload), (3) maps audit events to Rig Relay governance concepts (e.g., 'org.add_member' → tenant memberships, 'repo.change_visibility' → repo scope change detection), (4) surfaces in the cockpit Enterprise Audit widget with time-range filtering. Rate-limit polling to every 5 minutes with backoff. Store raw audit event JSON in a jsonb_envelope field for future schema evolution.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Do you ingest our GitHub audit log? Can you correlate audit events with code scanning findings? Do you support audit log streaming (not just polling)? Can we export audit events to our SIEM?' Expect procurement to require audit log ingestion as a precondition for security-team adoption.

sections.title: Multi-Org/Multi-Repo Portfolio Views
sections.current_state: The cockpit widgets (Provider Health, Repository Coverage, Mission Topology) are designed for single-installation views. No cross-org aggregation or portfolio dashboard exists. The _operating_picture.py generates a per-installation operating picture but does not union across installations.
sections.gap_analysis: Large enterprises operate dozens of GitHub orgs (engineering, data, infrastructure, security). Rig Relay currently treats each installation independently. No cross-org alert aggregation (e.g., 'Show me all critical code scanning alerts across all 12 orgs'). No portfolio-level risk heatmap. No org-comparison views for code-scanning maturity. The Postgres schema has tenant_repo_org_keys but no query layer that unions across these keys for portfolio views.
sections.required_implementation: Build a PortfolioAggregator that: (1) unions rows across installations using tenant_id and org_slug as grouping keys, (2) materializes a portfolio_summary materialized view in Postgres (with DuckDB projection for analytical queries), (3) generates a Portfolio Risk Heatmap widget (orgs on X axis, alert severity on Y axis, cell color by count), (4) adds portfolio-level trend lines (alert count over time, remediation rate per org, mean time to remediate). Add a Portfolio view mode to the cockpit (alongside Operator, Review, System, Technical). The portfolio view must respect tenant isolation (tenant_id scoping at every query).
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Can we see all our orgs in one dashboard? Can we compare security posture across business units? Can we export a portfolio PDF for our board meeting?' Large-enterprise procurement will demand portfolio views as a differentiator against single-org tools like GitHub Advanced Security's native dashboard.

sections.title: Team/Repo Permission Mapping
sections.current_state: No team-repo permission mapping exists. The _capabilities.py and _operating_picture.py ingest repo metadata but do not call the GitHub Teams API (GET /orgs/{org}/teams, GET /orgs/{org}/teams/{team_slug}/repos) to build a permission matrix.
sections.gap_analysis: Enterprises need to know: which teams have admin access to which repos? Which repos have no CODEOWNERS file? Where are external collaborators granted write access? Without team-repo mapping, Rig Relay cannot answer RBAC questions that security teams ask: 'Who can approve PRs on our production Terraform repos?' or 'Which repos have direct push access (no branch protection)?' This is a critical gap for the security-review use case.
sections.required_implementation: Add a TeamRepoPermissionIngestor that: (1) calls GET /orgs/{org}/teams with pagination, (2) for each team, calls /teams/{team_slug}/repos to fetch repo associations and permission levels, (3) stores in a github_team_repo_permission table (team_slug, repo_name, permission: admin|maintain|push|triage|pull), (4) cross-references with branch protection data to flag 'direct push without branch protection' repos, (5) cross-references with CODEOWNERS existence to flag repos missing ownership declarations. Surface in the cockpit as a Permission Matrix widget with filters by team, repo, and permission level. Generate a Permission Hygiene Report that ranks repos by risk (no CODEOWNERS + no branch protection + broad write access).
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Can you map our GitHub teams to repo permissions? Can you flag repos without CODEOWNERS? Can you integrate with our IdP to map GitHub teams to LDAP/Okta groups?' SOC2 and SOX auditors will require evidence of access review capabilities.

sections.title: SSO/SAML/SCIM-Adjacent Planning
sections.current_state: Rig Relay has OAuth-based identity (rig_relay/identity/) but no SAML, SCIM, or OIDC integration. The GitHub provider does not consume GitHub org SAML/SCIM data. No integration with enterprise IdPs (Okta, Azure AD, PingFederate) exists.
sections.gap_analysis: Enterprise GitHub orgs enforce SAML SSO. Rig Relay needs to understand the SAML identity layer to correctly attribute actions to human identities (not just GitHub handles). Without SCIM integration, user provisioning is manual. Without SAML attribute mapping, Rig Relay cannot map GitHub identities to corporate identities for audit purposes. The GitHub provider currently observes only GitHub-level identities (usernames), which don't correlate to corporate email/UPN for enterprise audit trails.
sections.required_implementation: Phase 1: Read-side only. Ingest GitHub org SAML identity mappings (GET /orgs/{org}/credential-authorizations) to build a github_identity → corporate_identity mapping table. Store SAML attributes (email, name_id, groups) in a github_saml_identity table. Cross-reference with audit events to attribute actions to corporate identities. Phase 2: Write-side. Add OIDC provider configuration for Rig Relay's own auth (so enterprises can SSO into the cockpit). Add SCIM provisioning endpoint for automated user lifecycle management. Surface SAML mapping coverage in the cockpit Identity widget.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Do you support SSO for the cockpit? Can you provision users via SCIM? Can you map GitHub handles to our Okta directory? Are you FedRAMP-ready for identity federation?' This is a P3 for observability but becomes P0 if Rig Relay is deployed as an enterprise-wide control-plane with multiple human operators.

sections.title: Branch Protection/Ruleset Policy Reporting
sections.current_state: The _capabilities.py declares a github_branch_protection observation capability. The _operating_picture.py can ingest branch protection rules via GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches?protected=true and GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets. The github_branch_protection_snapshot and github_ruleset_snapshot tables exist in the Postgres schema.
sections.gap_analysis: Ingestion exists but reporting is rudimentary. No policy-diff view (what changed between two snapshots?). No compliance scoring (e.g., '87% of repos require PR reviews'). No ruleset cross-reference with code scanning findings (e.g., 'Are repos with critical alerts missing required status checks?'). No drift detection (branch protection was enabled, someone disabled it via a GitHub admin action, Rig Relay should alert). No enforcement of org-level policies (all repos must have branch protection on main).
sections.required_implementation: Build a BranchProtectionPolicyReporter that: (1) computes a compliance score per repo (0-100) based on branch protection settings weightings (require_pr_review=30, require_status_checks=25, require_conversation_resolution=15, require_signed_commits=10, enforce_admins=10, lock_branch=5, require_deployments=5), (2) diffs consecutive snapshots and emits policy_drift alerts when protection is weakened, (3) cross-references with code scanning alert severity to compute a Protection Gap Score (critical alerts on repos with weak protection = high risk), (4) generates an org-level compliance report with remediation recommendations. Add a Branch Protection widget to the cockpit compact/standard/expanded disclosure levels. Store drift events in github_enterprise_audit_event with event_type='branch_protection.drift.detected'.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Can you report on our branch protection coverage? Can you detect when someone disables branch protection? Can you enforce org-level policies?' SOC2 auditors will ask for evidence that production repos have branch protection enforced. CISO reviews will demand drift alerts.

sections.title: Code Scanning/Secret Scanning/Dependabot Maturity
sections.current_state: The _code_scanning_source_context.py and related modules ingest code scanning alerts, secret scanning alerts, and Dependabot alerts via GitHub webhooks and REST API. The github_code_scanning_alert, github_secret_scanning_alert, and github_dependabot_alert tables exist. The _operating_picture.py projects these into the provider operating picture.
sections.gap_analysis: Ingestion is comprehensive but analysis maturity is low. No alert lifecycle tracking (when was this alert opened, dismissed, fixed, reopened?). No alert-trend dashboards (are we gaining or losing alerts over time?). No alert-autopsy correlation (which PR introduced the alert?). No cross-tool correlation (is this Dependabot alert related to a code scanning alert in the same file?). No SARIF rule coverage analysis (which CodeQL queries are used across the org? Are there gaps?). No false-positive/true-positive classification learned from dismissal reasons. No mean-time-to-remediate (MTTR) computation per team/repo/severity. No SLA tracking (critical alerts must be fixed in 7 days).
sections.required_implementation: Build an AlertMaturityAnalyzer with: (1) Alert Lifecycle Tracker that reconstructs state transitions from webhook events (created→dismissed→reopened→fixed→fixed again), (2) Alert Trend Engine computing weekly/daily alert counts by severity and tool with linear regression for trend direction, (3) Alert Autopsy correlator that matches alert introductions to PR merge events within a time window, (4) Cross-Tool Correlator that links code scanning + secret scanning + Dependabot alerts by file path and commit range, (5) SARIF Rule Coverage Reporter that enumerates active CodeQL queries per repo and flags missing rules based on a recommended rule set, (6) MTTR/SLA Tracker that computes remediation time per alert and flags SLA violations. Add Alert Maturity score (0-100) per repo computed from: alert-trend direction, MTTR, rule coverage percentage, false-positive ratio, and SLA compliance percentage.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How does this compare to GitHub Advanced Security's native dashboard? Does it track MTTR? Can it correlate alerts to PRs? Does it support custom SARIF rules? Can we define SLA policies per severity?' Security teams evaluating Rig Relay against GHAS native reporting will demand parity plus differentiation.

sections.title: Data Residency/Export/Delete Expectations
sections.current_state: Rig Relay stores all GitHub-derived data locally (Postgres, DuckDB, JSONL files under .rig/). No cloud-hosted storage exists. No data export or bulk-delete API exists. No data residency policy document exists.
sections.gap_analysis: GDPR and regional data-residency regulations require: right to access (export all data about a user), right to erasure (delete all data about a user within 30 days), data residency (keep data in a specific geographic region). Rig Relay stores data locally but has no programmatic export or selective-delete capability. The retention policies in the Postgres schema are conceptual but not enforced. No data classification labeling exists (PII, confidential, public). The JSONL artifacts under .rig/ are append-only with no deletion path.
sections.required_implementation: Add a DataGovernanceAPI with: (1) GET /api/data-export?entity=repo&id=X → streams all JSONL rows for that repo as a tar.gz with manifest, (2) DELETE /api/data-purge?entity=repo&id=X → marks all rows for retention expiry and schedules a GC pass, (3) GET /api/data-inventory → returns byte counts per table per tenant, (4) data classification tags on every table (see security_class field in Postgres schema), (5) a data-retention enforcement daemon that runs daily and hard-deletes rows past their retention window, (6) a Data Residency Policy document at docs/json/governance/data_residency_policy.v1.json. The local-deployment model simplifies residency (data never leaves the host), but export/delete must still be supported for compliance.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Where is our data stored? Can you export all data about a specific user? Can you delete data on request? Do you have a DPA (Data Processing Agreement)? Are you GDPR/CCPA compliant?' Procurement will require a DPA for cloud-hosted deployments; local-only deployments may be exempt but export/delete is still expected.

sections.title: Postgres Tenant/Org/Repo Boundaries
sections.current_state: The Postgres schema for GitHub-derived tables includes tenant_id, org_slug, and repo_name columns (tenant_repo_org_keys). Multi-tenant isolation exists in concept (tenant_id column) but row-level security (RLS) policies are not implemented. Query construction does not enforce tenant scoping via SET app.current_tenant_id.
sections.gap_analysis: Postgres is the enterprise operational substrate for indexed GitHub projections, but portable evidence remains JSON/JSONL/CSV. Product telemetry disabled must not disable enterprise GitHub audit/evidence continuity. Without RLS policies, a SQL injection or misconfigured query could cross tenant boundaries. The tenant_id column exists but is a convention, not a hard enforcement. Row-level security must be enforced at the database layer, not the application layer. No tenant-scoped connection pooling exists. No per-tenant storage quota tracking. No tenant data isolation test suite.
sections.required_implementation: Implement PostgreSQL Row-Level Security: (1) CREATE POLICY per table that enforces tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id'), (2) SET app.current_tenant_id at connection-pool checkout time, (3) add a tenant_isolation_test suite that attempts cross-tenant queries and asserts zero rows, (4) add per-tenant storage quota tracking in a tenant_quota table with enforcement at INSERT time, (5) add a Tenant Data Boundary Dashboard widget showing per-table row counts and byte sizes per tenant. The local-deployment model means one Postgres instance serves one tenant, reducing cross-tenant risk, but RLS must still be implemented as defense-in-depth.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How do you ensure one customer's data is never exposed to another? Do you use database-level tenant isolation? Can we have a dedicated Postgres instance?' For local deployments, this is lower risk but enterprises evaluating cloud-hosted Rig Relay will demand proof of tenant isolation.

sections.title: Procurement/Security Questionnaire Evidence
sections.current_state: No security questionnaire response pack exists. No SOC2 report. No penetration test report. No vulnerability disclosure program. No security.txt. No third-party dependency SBOM. The AGENTS.md, README.md, and usage-data-doctrine.md cover observable behavior but are not procurement-ready security artifacts.
sections.gap_analysis: Enterprise procurement processes require: (1) a completed CAIQ-Lite or SIG questionnaire, (2) a SOC2 Type II report (for cloud-hosted deployments), (3) a penetration test report from an accredited firm (within last 12 months), (4) a software bill of materials (SBOM in SPDX or CycloneDX format), (5) a vulnerability disclosure policy (security.txt), (6) a data flow diagram showing where GitHub data enters, is processed, and is stored, (7) a subprocessor list (if any cloud services are used), (8) a business continuity and disaster recovery plan. None of these exist for Rig Relay.
sections.required_implementation: Phase 1 - Self-Service Artifacts: (1) Generate an SBOM via 'uv run python scripts/rig_generate_sbom.py' that uses pip-audit or syft to enumerate dependencies, (2) Write a security.txt at docs/.well-known/security.txt with PGP key and disclosure policy, (3) Write a CAIQ-Lite self-assessment at docs/json/governance/caiq_lite_self_assessment.v1.json covering the 73 CAIQ-Lite controls, (4) Generate a data flow diagram as a Mermaid diagram in docs/json/architecture/data_flow_github_integration.v1.json. Phase 2 - Third-Party: Commission a penetration test and publish executive summary. Phase 3 - Continuous: Integrate SBOM generation into the release pipeline. Publish security posture at a public /security page on the docs site.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Do you have a SOC2 report? When was your last penetration test? Can you provide an SBOM? Where is your vulnerability disclosure policy? Do you have a data flow diagram?' Without these artifacts, enterprise procurement will stall at the security review stage regardless of technical capability.

sections.title: Rate-Limit Budgeting
sections.current_state: The _rate_limit_budget.py concept exists (github_rate_limit_budget table) but is not actively enforced. The provider packet ingestion polls GitHub APIs without rate-limit awareness beyond GitHub's built-in 403/429 handling. No pre-flight rate-limit check, no quota allocation across ingestion tasks, and no backpressure from rate-limit exhaustion exist.
sections.gap_analysis: GitHub's API rate limits vary: 5,000 requests/hour for personal tokens, 15,000/hour for GitHub App installations, 12,500/hour for GitHub Enterprise Server. Without rate-limit budgeting, a large org ingestion can exhaust the limit, starving other features (webhook processing, PR mutation, code scanning queries). No cost-attribution exists (which ingestion task consumed the most quota?). No adaptive sampling (skip low-priority repos when quota is low). No rate-limit forecast (will we exhaust the budget at current ingestion rate?).
sections.required_implementation: Build a RateLimitBudgetManager with: (1) Pre-flight check before every API call that queries current rate-limit status from GitHub (GET /rate_limit), (2) Quota allocation per ingestion task (repo scanning: 40%, audit log: 10%, code scanning: 25%, secret scanning: 15%, Dependabot: 10%) configurable per tenant, (3) Adaptive sampling that drops low-priority repos when budget drops below 20%, (4) Rate-limit cost attribution per task with a cost_center column in github_api_call_receipt, (5) Rate-limit forecast that uses linear regression on consumption velocity, (6) Rate-limit backpressure signal that pauses non-critical ingestion and emits a cockpit alert. Store budget snapshots every 5 minutes in github_rate_limit_budget. Surface in the cockpit as a Rate Limit Budget widget with a gauge visualization.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How many API calls do you make per hour? Can we set a cap? What happens if you hit the rate limit? Do you respect GitHub's secondary rate limits?' Large enterprises with 10,000+ repos will exhaust rate limits without budgeting. Procurement will demand rate-limit controls.

sections.title: Webhook Reliability and Replay
sections.current_state: The github_webhook_event table exists. The _operating_picture.py and related modules handle incoming webhooks but with no delivery-guarantee layer. No webhook signature verification. No webhook replay mechanism. No webhook delivery-lag monitoring. No dead-letter queue for failed webhook processing.
sections.gap_analysis: GitHub webhooks are at-most-once delivery. If Rig Relay is down during a webhook delivery, GitHub retries for 72 hours then drops the event. Without a replay buffer, missed events create gaps in the operating picture (e.g., a code scanning alert was dismissed but Rig Relay didn't see the webhook, so the alert appears stale forever). No idempotency key handling (X-GitHub-Delivery header) to prevent duplicate processing. No out-of-order detection (webhooks can arrive out of order, especially during bulk events).
sections.required_implementation: Build a WebhookReliabilityLayer with: (1) Webhook signature verification using HMAC-SHA256 with the GitHub App webhook secret (validate X-Hub-Signature-256 header on every inbound webhook), (2) Idempotency based on X-GitHub-Delivery GUID stored in a webhook_deduplication table with a 30-day TTL, (3) Out-of-order detection using the webhook payload timestamp vs. the last processed timestamp for that repo/event_type, (4) Dead-letter queue for webhooks that fail processing (retry 3x with exponential backoff, then quarantine), (5) Webhook replay from the GitHub API (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/hooks/{hook_id}/deliveries + redeliver) exposed as a cockpit action, (6) Webhook delivery statistics widget showing received/processed/failed/delayed counts per event_type, (7) Webhook gap detection that periodically compares webhook event IDs with the GitHub delivery log to identify missed events.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How do you handle missed webhooks? Can you replay webhooks? Do you verify webhook signatures? What happens if Rig Relay is down for an hour?' Security teams will demand guaranteed delivery for security-event webhooks (code scanning, secret scanning, Dependabot).

sections.title: Incident Investigation Timeline
sections.current_state: Raw data exists across github_api_call_receipt, github_webhook_event, github_enterprise_audit_event, and the JSONL artifact files. No unified timeline view exists. No correlation engine links events across tables. No incident investigation workflow.
sections.gap_analysis: When a security incident occurs (e.g., 'Someone pushed a secret to repo X at 3am'), the investigator needs to: see all PRs around that time, see code scanning alerts for that repo, see who had push access, see if branch protection was active, see the audit log for permission changes, see if Dependabot had flagged a vulnerable dependency in the same file. Currently, an investigator must manually query 8+ tables. No timeline stitching exists. No investigation notebook/workspace exists. No evidence-export for incident reports exists.
sections.required_implementation: Build an IncidentTimelineEngine that: (1) Accepts a time window and repo scope, (2) Queries all GitHub-derived tables and unions events into a unified timeline sorted by timestamp, (3) Tags each event with event_type, actor, repo, and a relevance_score (0-1) based on correlation rules, (4) Generates an Incident Timeline JSON artifact at .build/rig-relay/evidence/incident_timeline_{incident_id}.v1.json, (5) Renders a static HTML timeline for sharing with incident response teams, (6) Surfaces in the cockpit as an Investigation Mode (a special layout with a horizontal timeline scrubber and event cards). Use the existing github_evidence_timeline table as the backing store. Add an investigative notebook feature that lets operators pin events, add notes, and export a curated timeline.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Can we investigate incidents across all our GitHub orgs? Can we export a timeline for our incident report? Can we correlate GitHub events with our SIEM?' Incident response teams will demand a unified timeline view for post-mortem investigations.

sections.title: Backup/Restore of GitHub-Derived Projections
sections.current_state: GitHub-derived data lives in Postgres tables, DuckDB files, and JSONL artifacts under .rig/. No automated backup exists. No point-in-time recovery exists. No backup integrity verification. No backup retention policy.
sections.gap_analysis: If the Postgres data directory or DuckDB file is corrupted, all projections are lost. GitHub data can be re-ingested, but re-ingesting 5,000 repos with code scanning alerts takes hours and burns rate-limit budget. The JSONL artifacts serve as a low-level backup but with no restore tooling (you'd have to manually replay JSONL files into Postgres). No backup for the content-light normalized JSONL files themselves. No WAL archiving for Postgres.
sections.required_implementation: Build a ProjectionBackupManager that: (1) Performs daily pg_dump of GitHub-derived tables (excluding raw JSONB envelopes for storage efficiency, keeping typed columns + foreign keys), (2) Copies the DuckDB database file and JSONL artifact directory to a backup location, (3) Verifies backup integrity by computing SHA256 of backup files and comparing with a manifest, (4) Retains backups per policy (daily: 7 days, weekly: 4 weeks, monthly: 12 months), (5) Provides a restore CLI: 'uv run rig-relay restore-github-projections --date 2026-05-15' that recreates Postgres tables and DuckDB from backup, (6) Excludes the backup feature from the GitHub rate-limit budget (uses local I/O only). Surface backup status in the cockpit System widget (last backup time, size, integrity check result).
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'How do you back up our GitHub data? What's your RPO/RTO? Can we restore to a point in time? Do you encrypt backups at rest?' SOC2 and ISO 27001 require documented backup and restore procedures with tested recovery.

sections.title: Hosted vs Local Deployment Model
sections.current_state: Rig Relay is local-first. It runs on the user's machine with local Postgres/DuckDB/JSONL storage. No cloud-hosted deployment exists. No SaaS offering. The README positions it as a desktop application with a local server/control-plane.
sections.gap_analysis: Enterprise deployment should support read-only observer profile as default. No write access to GitHub without explicit admin configuration. Local deployment is a strength for security (data never leaves the user's machine) but a weakness for enterprise adoption (no centralized administration, no shared dashboard, no fleet-wide visibility). Enterprises want: a centralized deployment that multiple security-team members can access, a single source of truth for GitHub security posture across all orgs, and admin controls over who can see/do what. The local model also means no SLAs, no uptime guarantees, and no managed service. The governance model (AGENTS.md) assumes single-user desktop operation, not multi-user enterprise deployment.
sections.required_implementation: Define a Deployment Model Matrix: (A) Local Desktop — current model, single user, local storage, no multi-tenancy needed, (B) Local Server — headless server mode (rig-relay --server-only), multiple browser clients connecting via WebSocket, still single-machine but multi-user, needs auth and RBAC, (C) Cloud-Hosted — managed SaaS, multi-tenant Postgres, cloud storage for artifacts, needs SOC2, uptime SLA, DPA, subprocessor list. Document the deployment model trade-offs in docs/json/architecture/deployment_model_matrix.v1.json. For (B), implement: cockpit auth (OIDC), RBAC role mapping (viewer, analyst, operator, admin), session management, and per-user permission scoping. For (C), this is a P4 until there's market demand. Position (B) as the enterprise-ready deployment model.
sections.procurement_implications: Enterprises will ask: 'Is this SaaS or on-prem? Can we self-host? Can we deploy in our VPC? Do you offer a managed cloud version? What are your uptime SLAs?' The answer shapes procurement entirely: self-hosted avoids DPA/SOC2 but requires the enterprise to manage infrastructure. Cloud-hosted requires SOC2, DPA, uptime SLA, and subprocessor transparency.
